questions.q: Using b1=[1,1] and b2=[1,-1], solving a+b=5 and a-b=1 for the vector [5,1] gives which coefficients?
questions.explain: Adding the two equations gives 2a=6 so a=3, then substituting gives b=2; checking, 3*[1,1]+2*[1,-1] = [5,1], matching the target vector.

questions.q: For the change-of-basis matrix P = [[1,1],[1,-1]], what is det(P)?

questions.explain: Using the 2x2 inverse formula with det=-2: P^-1 = (1/-2)*[[-1,-1],[-1,1]] = [[0.5,0.5],[0.5,-0.5]], which was verified by multiplying it against [5,1] to recover [3,2].

questions.q: Why must the basis vectors go into the change-of-basis matrix as columns, not rows?
options: Rows are only used for 3x3 matrices, columns only for 2x2
It makes no difference whether they are rows or columns
Because putting them in as rows produces a different (transposed) matrix whose inverse will not correctly convert coordinates
Because row vectors cannot be inverted
questions.explain: The change-of-basis matrix is defined with basis vectors as columns; using rows instead transposes the matrix, giving an incorrect result when you compute its inverse and apply it.

questions.q: What does changing a qubit's state from the computational basis {|0>,|1>} to the {|+>,|-> } basis represent mathematically?
options: The same operation as normalization from Lesson 3
The same change-of-basis operation practiced in this lesson: the same underlying state gets different coordinates when expressed relative to a different basis
A physical change to the qubit itself, altering what state it is in
An operation that is only possible for multi-qubit systems
questions.explain: Expressing the same physical qubit state in a different basis is exactly a change of basis -- the underlying vector doesn't change, but its coordinate representation does, converted using a matrix inverse as practiced in this lesson.
